title: 25-year Amazon drought experiment reveals rainforest's vulnerability to extreme conditions
summary: The 25-year Esecaflor Project in Brazil's Amazon, which diverted 50% of rainwater from a one-hectare study area since 2001, shows significant die-off of large trees and potential transformation into a degraded forest ecosystem rather than savanna. The experimental structure was removed two years ago
takeaways: Duration: 25 years (started 2001); structure removed ~2 years ago (2024)
Method: 6,000 transparent plastic panels diverting ~50% rainfall for 2 decades
Outcome: significant large-tree die-off; forest shifted to new equilibrium (degraded forest, not savanna)
Longest-running, most extensive tropical forest drought study conducted
Monitoring: soil, air, tree growth, sap flow, roots; two 40-meter towers with NASA radar

title: Simultaneous heat waves and wildfire smoke exposure surging to affect over 1 billion annually
summary: More than 1 billion people per year were exposed to concurrent heat waves and wildfire smoke from 2010–2019, according to Science Advances research led by Monash University. takeaways: Over 1 billion people annually exposed to concurrent heat and wildfire smoke 2010–2019
Sharp increase from previous decade 2000–2009
Growth driven by increased frequency of dual exposure, not population growth alone
Largest global assessment to date of simultaneous heat and wildfire exposure
Coexposure to heatwaves and wildfire smoke increased from 2000–2019
Study analyzed global population simultaneously facing both hazards

takeaways: Lula reelected October 25, 2026, defeating Flávio Bolsonaro-aligned candidate

title: Bird Flu Causes Catastrophic Wildlife Die-Offs, Raising Extinction Risk Concerns
summary: Bird flu (H5N1) has triggered catastrophic wildlife die-offs, prompting the IUCN to upgrade the southern elephant seal to vulnerable status in April 2026—the first species explicitly downgraded due to avian influenza. On South Georgia, more than 53,000 female seals died by 2025.
takeaways: H5N1 now conservation threat to at least 40 bird species (BirdLife International)
Southern elephant seal: first species upgraded to vulnerable explicitly due to avian influenza

title: Afghan Families Forced to Marry Off Girls as Climate Drought Deepens

summary: The president of the United States administration cut federal NOAA funding dramatically after taking office in 2025, reducing grant awards by 74% to 229 by September 2, 2026 compared to an average of 891 in prior years. title: Rapid coral bleaching recovery via symbiont transfer from healthy corals
summary: A study in Frontiers in Conservation Science describes methods to accelerate coral recovery from bleaching by transferring symbiotic algae and bacteria from healthy colonies to bleached corals. Physical contact between healthy and bleached corals can restore color within five days.

Physical contact between healthy and bleached corals restores color in five days

title: Conservationists rescue 3,400 rare one-flowered wintergreens from eroding Scottish coastline

title: Sea Level Rise Could Displace Habitats of Over 42% of Land Vertebrates
summary: A Science study of 34,120 species found climate-driven sea level rise could cause habitat loss for over 42% of terrestrial vertebrates by 2100. Between 14,325 and 15,324 species will lose habitat across IPCC scenarios, though only 5.9% are currently listed as at-risk.
takeaways: 42% of terrestrial land vertebrates face habitat loss by 2100
14,325–15,324 species affected depending on climate scenario (5 IPCC scenarios examined)
Up to 63% birds, 52% mammals, 36% reptiles, 24% amphibians affected
Amazon River delta and Southeast Asia face most significant losses; 96% refuge areas outside protected areas
